A4.v: This is a Table Based Model (TBM) re-engineered version of CFI's Three Statement Model. It is designed to illustrate how TBM works in the context of Financial Modeling (FM)

A7.v: TBM provides many benefits that become more important as models become larger and more complex. This is because tables mimic the databases that all ERPs and other business systems use. By leveraging the vast knowledge of database design we can structure our models so they adapt just like ERPs adapt to all sorts of businesses and accounting practices. This flexibility simply is not practical with traditional FM methodologies.

A11.v: IPO has a different meaning in computer science. It stands for Input-Process-Output model. CFI's model doesn't follow this principal. It is a single sheet model which is well suited for simple models like this one. So this isn't a great example to show the positive aspects of TBM. But because it is simple, it is a great tool to explain some concepts. A foundational concept in computer science is this: Inputs should be kept separate from processes to prevent accidental change of formulas and outputs are separate from processes to allow any number of lists, reports, or charts over the same calculation set. Essentially, the process is the single version of truth that all outputs pull from.

A12.v: Many complex FM's keep inputs separate, and use worksheets, or even workbooks, to segregate logical components. But it wasn't until 2003 that MS added 'Lists', which became 'Tables' in 2007 and modeling gained a new structure to help organize models

A14.v: Tables have names allowing us to label our model structures like: Assumptions, Income Statement, Cash Flow Statement, etc. This is a tremendous help during development and review because names can convey subject and intent as-well-as we can leverage F5 to goto any of these structures without having to use name manager to create a name. CFI's model uses headings to convey calculations blocks but to support F5 (Go To) functions we must name the headings, which CFI does not. And if CFI's model needed to use references on a different worksheet, CFI's formulas would need to include the worksheet name. TBM formulas use table names instead and it makes no difference which worksheet the table is currently on, or moved to.

A16.v: Tables have 'Structured References' which adds names to table sections, like table columns. With TBM's structured references we can use table names like named variables in formulas instead of CFI's cryptic cell references. This makes TBM's formulas self-documenting and much easier to understand intent.

A18.v: Excel's tables are dynamic named ranges. Only Excel's dynamic arrays can match table's flexibility. TBM can effortlessly expand to accommodate any number of attributes such as periods, dimensions, customers, accounts, products, etc. CFI's structure makes such tasks extremely difficult and error prone.

A20.v: BXL's implementation of TBM uses lookup techniques to find values. CFI uses point-to cell references. The point-to style can break when we don't pay attention to Excel's absolute, relative, and mixed referencing. BXL's lookup style makes expanding/contracting components or moving components anywhere in the workbook a non-issue.

A22.v: Any model, financial or otherwise, is made better with analytics. TBMs are perfectly suited for basic analytics such as sorting, aggregating (pivots), filtering (Slicers) and dynamic charting (Pivot Charts). They are also perfectly suited for exporting to more specialized analytical tools.

A24.v: As mentioned earlier, all business computer systems (Treasury, Accounting, HRIS, Payroll, MRP, etc.) use databases and Excel's tables mimic those databases on a smaller scale. That makes tables perfect for importing actuals from, or exporting forecast to those systems. It also makes them perfect for working with Microsoft's PowerQuery, Power Pivot, and Power BI tools.

A26.v: TBM shines when models get larger and more complex because tables add structure and labeling which is critical to a project's development, review, and maintenance phases. They also integrate with other systems making leveraging recorded data (ex. Actuals) more timely and less prone to data entry errors. Lastly, TBMs are unmatched in their ability to accommodate changes such as added periods, accounts, customers, companies, etc.
